bull.b: Record IET bookings and a $37.1 billion RPO provide substantial multi-year revenue visibility. This backlog supports capacity planning, improves confidence in future equipment and service demand, and strengthens Baker Hughes’ position across LNG, power and industrial infrastructure markets.

Expanding EBITDA margins alongside robust free cash flow indicates improving operating execution and meaningful internal funding capacity. Sustained profitability can support investment, debt reduction and shareholder returns while giving the company greater resilience through cyclical energy markets.

The Chart acquisition broadens Baker Hughes beyond traditional oilfield exposure into thermal management, industrial infrastructure and emissions-related applications. Cross-selling and planned synergies could make revenue more diversified and increase the contribution from resilient aftermarket and service activities.

bear.b: The sharp increase in debt relative to equity reduces financial flexibility and raises sensitivity to downturns in cyclical energy markets. Although management plans to deleverage, elevated leverage can constrain capital allocation and increase the importance of sustained cash generation after the acquisition.

A sharply negative trailing revenue trend raises questions about the consistency of top-line expansion, even as margins remain solid. Uneven revenue growth can make utilization and earnings less predictable, limiting the durability of recent profitability if demand or project timing weakens.

Strong order intake does not translate immediately into reported revenue because longer GTE cycles and aero-derivative supply-chain timing defer conversion. This creates a gap between backlog visibility and near-term growth, increasing dependence on execution and future project timing.
